title: The Forgetting-Retention Dilemma: Certified Unlearning Theory in Continual Learning
claim: Sequential learning and certified deletion form a two-stage loop in which each updated model feeds the next task.
layout: Single row, left-to-right, two dashed-box stages with inputs dropping onto modules
description: A horizontal flow diagram that reads left to right. It starts with a light-blue model box w_{t-1}^{-S_{1:t-1}}. A black arrow leads into a dashed rounded box labeled in red 'Stage I: learning on new task'. Inside, a green 'Task t: D_t' box sends a blue arrow down into a peach module 'ℓ2-CL(·, D_t)', which outputs a blue model box w_t^{-S_{1:t-1}}. The arrow continues into a second dashed box, 'Stage II: Unlearning on new deletion request'. There a green 'Request: S_t' box feeds a peach module 'R_A(·, D_{1:t}, S_{1:t})'. The arrow then enters a gray dashed region titled '(ε,δ)-certified...', where the crop cuts off the output models. Blue boxes are models, green boxes are inputs, and peach boxes are operations. Red bold stage titles draw the eye first.
caption: Two-stage CL and unlearning at time \(t\): starting from the last model $w_{t-1}^{-S_{1:t-1}}$ at time $t-1$, we first train on task \(t\) with dataset $D_t$ to obtain \(w_t^{-S_{1:t-1}}\) in Stage I. Upon receiving a possible deletion request \(S_t\), in Stage II, the unlearning scheme \(\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal A}(\cdot, D_{1:t}, S_{1:t})\) in ([ref]) updates the internal model \( w_t^{-S_{1:t}}\), and publishes the final unlearning model \(\tilde w_t^{-S_{1:t}}\), by noise adding mapping $f$ in ([ref]) to achieve \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-certified continual unlearning in Definition [ref]. Then, it feeds \( w_t^{-S_{1:t}}\) to train on next task \(t+1\).
abstract: Machine unlearning aims to eliminate the influence of specific data from trained models to safeguard privacy. However, this presents a significant challenge in the context of continual learning (CL), where models update sequentially on dynamic datasets. A major limitation is that current certified unlearning algorithms fail to account for the complex, cumulative model evolution inherent to CL framework. In this work, we establish the first theoretical foundation bridging CL and machine unlearning. We formulate the CL's unlearning objective as the minimization of post-unlearning excess risk, which decomposes into CL excess risk and unlearning loss, characterizing the fundamental trade-off between preserving historical knowledge and targeted forgetting. Under mild assumptions, we first establish an upper bound for the CL excess risk in non-convex models. We then adapt two certified unlearning approaches, gradient-based and Hessian-based, to the CL framework. Our analysis reveals that while the gradient-based approach is less effective than the Hessian-based method in minimizing unlearning loss, it offers the distinct advantage of nearly zero storage overhead for enabling unlearning. This insight motivates a hybrid strategy that reduces storage costs while maintaining post-unlearning performance. Experimental results further validate our theoretical findings.
